speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While our legal sector is relatively small, over the last 10 years, we were able to go beyond our shores, ride the wave of rising inter- and intra-Asia trade and investment and establish for ourselves a global brand name as a trusted location for high-quality cross-border dispute resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: We are trusted, not only because of our legal expertise, but also because people know that we are, and will remain, neutral, and that our legal regime is stable.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Strengthening our position as an international dispute resolution centre will benefit Singaporeans and Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, it helps create growth and jobs for Singapore law firms and lawyers, amidst a more challenging economic environment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, exposure to more, and more wide-ranging, legal work helps broaden and deepen the legal expertise available for domestic cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Third, our position as a legal service hub will bolster Singapore's overall attractiveness as a business hub and create value for other parts of the economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In Singapore, we provide a full suite of dispute resolution services so that businesses can pick and choose the services that best meet their particular needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mediation is one such service, complementing Court litigation and arbitration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It provides a more cost-effective, flexible and faster means of settling disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mediation is also well-suited to our Asian context, where harmony and amicable resolution are valued highly in the dispute resolution process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is particularly attractive for parties who desire to preserve long-term relationships and continue to do business.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In 2013, the Chief Justice and the Ministry of Law (MinLaw) set up an International Commercial Mediation Working Group to look into developing the international commercial mediation space in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Arising from the Working Group's recommendations, in 2014, the Ministry set up the Singapore International Mediation Centre (SIMC) and the Singapore International Mediation Institute (SIMI).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Part of SIMC's success lies in its strong focus on meeting the needs of businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For example, SIMC has worked across institutional boundaries, to partner the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) to develop the SIAC-SIMC arb-med-arb, an innovative protocol that offers businesses the option of both arbitration and mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: SIMI works closely with more than 20 domestic and international organisations to promote mediation and set high competency standards in mediation practice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Besides building strong institutions, Singapore needs a legislative framework for mediation if we desire to be an international centre for commercial mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Its provisions will strengthen the enforceability of a mediated settlement agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: They will also provide much-valued certainty for cross-border mediation users, in areas where the common law position is unclear or differs from jurisdiction to jurisdiction.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill will implement the last of the recommendations made by the International Commercial Mediation Working Group.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Its provisions incorporate inputs from public consultation and extensive stakeholder engagement with lawyers, mediation and alternative dispute resolution practitioners and service providers, academics and mediation professional bodies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The stakeholders we consulted are very much looking forward to this new legislation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It will help draw even more international commercial mediation work to Singapore and further strengthen Singapore's position as an international dispute resolution hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Bill will apply to mediations which are conducted wholly or partly in Singapore; or internationally, where the agreement to mediate provides that Singapore law or the Bill, if passed, should apply.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Minister is also able, on consultation with the Chief Justice, to extend any provision of the Bill to any mediation conducted by or under the direction of a Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To prevent inconsistencies with existing mediation legislation and frameworks, for instance, community mediations governed by the Community Mediation Centres Act, mediation processes conducted under, or provided by or under any written law, will be excluded.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the same way, the Minister may, where appropriate, also exclude specified mediation proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The key features of the Bill are to strengthen the enforceability of settlement agreements resulting from mediation; clarify confidentiality and admissibility rules; provide for stay of Court proceedings; and make clear that the restrictions under the Legal Profession Act do not apply under certain circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I will now take the House through these four key aspects.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The first key aspect of the Bill relates to strengthening the enforceability of mediated settlement agreements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The lack of enforceability of a mediated settlement agreement is an oft-cited concern of mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To illustrate, having gone through significant time and effort in a mediation, parties may finally reach a settlement agreement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, if one party later reneges on his obligations, the innocent party needs to commence Court proceedings, firstly, to prove a contract exists and, secondly, that the terms have been breached.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This lack of enforceability is seen as an inhibiting factor in attracting commercial parties to mediate a dispute, since finality and certainty of dispute resolution outcomes is key.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It does not alter or restrict the Court's existing powers to record a settlement agreement as a consent order, in cases where the dispute is already before the Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The additional expedited method provided by the Bill is as follows.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, once parties reach settlement, subject to the Bill's requirements, parties may further agree to apply to Court to have the settlement agreement recorded as a Court order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: To use this procedure, all parties to the agreement must agree to the application being made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such safeguards aim to ensure that the quality of the mediated settlement agreement is appropriate for being recorded and enforced as a Court order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Court may refuse to record the settlement agreement as a Court order under certain circumstances, for example, if this is contrary to public policy, if the subject matter of the agreement is not capable of settlement, if any term is not capable of enforcement as an order of Court and so on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Parties who are not able to use this procedure, for example, because other parties refuse to consent to the application, will still be able to commence court proceedings to enforce the settlement agreement as a contract.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Consequential and related amendments are made to the Supreme Court of Judicature Act and Family Justice Act to make clear that the Court has jurisdiction to record such mediated settlement agreements as Court orders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The second set of key provisions relate to confidentiality and admissibility of mediation communications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These positions seek to reflect current practices and expectations of mediation users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Confidentiality and privilege are considered key cornerstones of the mediation process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Today, however, such rules are based on a mixture of common law privileges, contractual protections and equitable remedies for breach of confidence.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In practice, parties may not be clear on how such protections apply to their individual circumstances.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Under the Bill, a protected mediation communication includes anything said or done, documents prepared or information provided in the course or for the purpose of the mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This also includes the agreement to mediate, and the settlement agreement, if any.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mediation communications are protected in two broad ways under the Bill.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: First, a mediation communication cannot be disclosed to any third party to the mediation, unless this falls under one of the listed exceptions, for example, party consent, or for the purpose of requesting legal advice and so on.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Short of these exceptions, any further disclosure will require the leave of Court, or an arbitral tribunal if the request for disclosure is being made in the context of arbitral proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The usual civil remedies for a breach of confidentiality will be available if unauthorised disclosure is made or threatened.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Second, a mediation communication is not to be admitted into evidence in any Court, arbitral or disciplinary proceedings, except with the leave of a Court or arbitral tribunal.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The third key aspect of the Bill is a provision to stay Court proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The Court may subject the stay order to any terms and conditions as it thinks fit and make further orders to preserve the rights of parties.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The provision will provide parties to a mediation with assurance that their legal position in any Court proceeding can be preserved pending the outcome of mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The fourth key aspect of the Bill is amendments to the Legal Profession Act, which make it clear that the restrictions on the practice of Singapore law will not apply to the mediation context where the mediation is conducted by (a) a certified mediator; or (b) administered by a designated mediation service provider.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: These are similar to existing provisions for arbitration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Such provisions will support international commercial mediation in Singapore by providing flexibility for parties intending to mediate to choose their own mediators and counsel, and encourage foreign mediators and counsel to use Singapore as a venue for mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With a strong base of legal talent, high-quality dispute resolution service providers and standard-setting professional bodies, the Bill will serve to create a more conducive environment in Singapore for international commercial mediation and reinforce Singapore's position as a premier venue for the conduct of international commercial mediation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I support the objectives of the Bill, including the economic objectives outlined by the learned Senior Minister of State earlier in her speech.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I take this opportunity to seek clarification on the policy underpinnings of the Bill in two areas.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With the recent launches of SIMC and the Singapore International Mediation Institute, we have made much further inroads into encouraging mediation as a cost- effective form of dispute resolution for potential litigants and in attracting such work into Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Indeed, I note that the Courts are now empowered to take the parties' conduct, including conduct in relation to whether the disputes were or were not submitted to mediation, into account when making decisions about costs at the end of proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In a parallel development in the United Kingdom (UK) occurring in July last year, it was recommended by Lord Justice Briggs in his Final Report of the UK Civil Courts Structure Review that "resolution by parties   a normal part of civil dispute resolution, rather than something alternative to the mainstream." In his words, the recommendation seeks to "take the 'A' out of ADR", or alternative dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, in Singapore, a party wishing to mediate has to either obtain the agreement of the other party to suspend the limitation period, or to first commence proceedings and seek a stay of proceedings while the mediation takes place.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In contrast, pursuant to the European Union (EU) Mediation Directive applicable to cross-border disputes, EU member states are required to ensure that the limitation period shall be extended during the period of the mediation process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Some criticism may be levied that allowing the limitation period to be suspended while mediation takes place may be abused by parties as a tactical manoeuvre to buy more time to commence a claim.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While this is possible, I wish to highlight that mediation is, at its core, a voluntary process.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It is open to a party to withdraw from a mediation process if it is of the view that the other party is not genuinely interested in mediating to resolve the dispute amicably, or it is using the mediation process to obtain an advantage in respect of the limitation period.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While we should not go so far as to mandate mediation before litigation as this would be an unwarranted restraint on an individual's right of access to Court, we should do as much as possible to encourage pre-action mediation and incentivise parties to do so.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Second, with respect to litigants who are represented by the Legal Aid Bureau in civil claims not involving family matters, I note that, pursuant to section 16(1) of the Legal Aid and Advice Act, aided persons are generally not liable to pay legal costs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is, therefore, no structural incentive for legally aided persons to mediate their disputes that are the subject of Court proceedings.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In addition, legal aid is granted only in relation to civil proceedings in the Courts under the First Schedule to the Legal Aid and Advice Act, not mediation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I further suggest that it be provided that aided persons in pending Court proceedings be obliged to comply with advice by their assigned solicitors to submit their cases for mediation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To conclude, I believe the Mediation Bill will achieve the objectives of enhancing and strengthening the mediation framework in Singapore to facilitate the resolution of disputes by mediation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill should be welcomed and I think I speak on behalf of all the legal academics that I can think of, to say that mediation has been often proposed as a form of dispute resolution that has been described as the poorer cousin of dispute resolution when compared to litigation and arbitration.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But seeing people like Mr Joel Lee, Chairman of the Singapore International Mediation Institute (SIMI), chairing it, we have a lot of encouragement and hope.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This Bill should be welcomed, not only because it codifies the definitions that we are used to as lawyers and the principles of mediation and mediation agreement, and the mediation settlement agreement, but also because it provides clarity on the position of mediation in relation to litigation and arbitration.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that is commonplace in the arbitration context, but is not so well-known in the mediation one.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 12 responds to a complaint that counsel and clients often level at mediation, as the Senior Minister of State mentioned earlier.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Importantly, clause 12(4) gives the Court useful guidance as to the circumstances when it can, in its discretion, refuse to record a mediated settlement agreement.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This is something that mediation shares with arbitration.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This will certainly add certainty to the law of mediation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Having said this, Madam, I would like to ask the following questions of the Ministry in clarification.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: First, in response to feedback during the public consultations, the Ministry responded to say that the Bill "does not seek to regulate the conduct of mediation itself, or set out mediator standards".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask the Senior Minister of State: will ethical breaches in mediation, such as conflicts of interest, impartiality and even mediator competence, be left to the Courts alone?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Or should this, in time, be something that the Ministry could envision being resolved by committees established by SIMC, SMC or SIM, as the designated mediation service providers and mediation institutions respectively?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I ask this as well, as this seems to be a direction that arbitration seems to be headed in − looking to the chartered institutes as a training body, resolving some conflict of interest problems, as opposed to having it always decided by the institutions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In some respects, Madam, this Bill seems to be a nod to the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law (UNCITRAL) Model Law on International Commercial Conciliation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What is the Ministry's position on the proposed UNCITRAL Convention on Enforcement of Conciliated Settlement Agreements?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: In the meantime, while we are waiting for such a convention to come about, how does the Ministry believe that the SIAC-SIMC arb-med-arb, which the Senior Minister of State mentioned, could provide the requisite basis to secure appropriate enforcement?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore prides itself on having a clear and distinct mediation framework that effectively resolves disputes or conflicts in a smooth, expeditious and cost-effective manner.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Government has also been actively promoting mediation in Singapore and encouraging parties to resolve disputes through mediation rather than litigation or arbitration.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In industrial relations disputes, cases are resolved through negotiations between two parties and if this comes to no avail, the dispute is being sought for third-party mediation, so that issues are resolved without further damage and to arrive at a win-win outcome.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: For example, it would exclude workplace disputes involving executive employees and their employers as there are provisions for tripartite mediation of disputes involving executive employees under the Industrial Relations Act.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, are family disputes also excluded from this Bill as there are laws covering mediation referred by the Family Justice Courts and mediation for commercial disputes are also covered by the Small Claims Tribunals?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What roles do the SMC or SIMC play with reference to the Bill?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will they be considered as the "designated mediation service providers" under this Bill?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Do the mediation procedures of the Singapore Mediation Centre apply in this Bill?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Bill require the presence of lawyers representing the interests of the parties involved in drafting the mediation agreement?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Born out of the recommendation by the Working Group for International Commercial Mediation, this Bill is a welcome move to advance the standing of mediation as a choice mode of alternative dispute resolution in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In practice, I have seen the fruits of mediation and experienced hearings before excellent mediators at the SMC and SIMC.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would not have been possible without the support and collaboration of MinLaw to promote Singapore as an international mediation centre.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is with much foresight that the Government and the Judiciary promoted mediation as a choice alternative dispute resolution mechanism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mediation places a priority on the reconciliation of relationships and, from my experience, this is very useful.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even though the main litigation is hard-fought, when mediation is attempted in parallel, parties sometimes settle.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When that happens, there is a win-win for all, companies and individuals alike.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If the mediation does not yield a settlement, the suit continues and rights are adjudicated at trial.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: MinLaw lent valuable support to the mediation movement by forming the Community Mediation Unit within the Ministry and an Alternative Dispute Resolution resource panel.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The panel sought to promote mediation in a wide variety of settings and comprised members of varied background.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: SMC was started in 1997 and plays an important role in Singapore's mediation landscape.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In 2013, the mediation movement sought to further promote the mediation in international commercial disputes.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have seen the fruits of the first two of the recommendations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Through excellent teamwork, Singapore mediation power houses in the like of SIMC and SIMI uphold the standard of our mediation services.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is on top of the excellent SMC, CMC and Court-based State Court Centre for Dispute Resolution, among others.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Today is, therefore, the time to make the next step, to buttress the current advantages that mediation lends to Singapore as a legal hub.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because mediation is an excellent forum for parties to come together on a non-adversarial platform to understand and resolve the underlying issues that bear on the case.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, having a co-mediator which allows industry experts to weigh in on the matter or ensuring that communications are without prejudice, which disarms parties and promotes a conciliatory approach, or, and importantly, having control over the outcome.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These and others culminate to facilitate a possible settlement agreement that is agreeable to all parties.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To solve this problem, SIMC has resorted to the SIMC-SIAC arb-med-arb protocol.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The option not to stay an action while mediation is carried out is a valuable tool in litigation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the clock ticking, the parties may have more incentive to settle in mediation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If a stay was made mandatory, then there would be little incentive to settle the matter promptly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With no timelines due, no affidavits to file, parties would not have the incentive to enter into mediation quickly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thus, parallel proceedings, running in tandem with any scheduled mediation hearing, may actually prompt settlement.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In closing, no emphasis on mediation should remove the parties' right to have their rights and duties adjudicated at the full trial.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As I understand it, this Bill does not intend to remove a right to a full trial if a company or private citizen seeks it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As such, and for reasons I have explained, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I applaud the work done by the International Commercial Mediation Working Group in putting together these recommendations.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Most notably, I welcome the provisions for parties to apply for stay of Court proceedings and defining the scope of confidentiality of these proceedings.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that while the mediation process has always been regarded as confidential, the scope of confidentiality was unclear.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, the Bill also codifies the circumstances under which disclosure may take place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I also welcome the proposal to extend the existing Legal Profession Act exceptions applicable to arbitration, to mediation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Mediation, unlike arbitration, is not commonly understood to involve the practice of law and often does not refer to legal principles at all.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Nonetheless, in certain cases, the relevant law may be discussed during the mediation session.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, the Bill mentions that the Court may refuse to record a mediated settlement if the subject matter is incapable of settlement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This provision seems to envisage that some matters may not be settled through mediation, for example, a mediated settlement on the custody of a child that may not be in the interest of the child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But it is the view of some mediators that all cases can be settled through mediation.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Would the Ministry be able to provide more clarity on which cases it envisages to be unsuitable for mediation?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I ask this with the knowledge that the Bill covers third-party funding for international arbitration proceedings and related proceedings, which also include mediation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: I rise in support of this Bill which seeks to promote, encourage and facilitate the resolution of disputes by mediation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: SIMI was incorporated in 2014 as a non-profit organisation supported by MinLaw to set up professional standards for mediators further to the International Commercial Mediation Working Group's recommendations to develop Singapore into a centre for international commercial mediation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Based on the offerings stated on SIMI's website, SIMI's work is primarily focused on accrediting at the moment although it also states that it aims to apply and enforce world-class standards of mediation, to make tools available to parties to make basic decisions about mediation and to promote mediation education and awareness.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: At the Singapore Mediation Lecture in 2013, Lord Woolf said that "There is a need for the continual appraisal of mediators who are accredited".

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Mediation has come a long way but it is still a journey.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The field now needs to evolve quickly into a true profession.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: High minimum practice and ethical standards need to be set, made transparent and achieved internationally.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Users of mediation need to see these standards operating effectively.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: More and better information needs to be made available by individual mediators about their skills, capabilities and personalities.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Quality and transparency together will enable mediation to grow.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Mediators, too, need to be suitably recognised for their expertise and skills.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With the passing of the Mediation Bill and, in light of clause 12, there is now a greater need to set standards, increase transparency and ensure the continual appraisal of accredited mediators through professional bodies.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The professional bodies can also determine the threshold and, where needed, investigate into whether the mediation or mediator falls below the requisite standards.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This, in turn, gives credibility to the profession and builds confidence in using mediation as an alternative dispute resolution mechanism.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: This is bearing in mind the limited number of accredited mediators and also the areas or topics of mediation work which is availed to enhance the experience and currency of their mediation work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The second suggestion is the grievance system to deal with complaints about mediation and mediators.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: With increased use of mediation, sooner or later, complaints against mediators may arise.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Having a grievance system in place gives confidence to parties agreeing to resolve their dispute via mediation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: The grievance system will also complement the accreditation and/or possible self-regulation efforts of professional bodies to raise standards.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: Having a professional body implement a grievance system to deal with complaints about mediators also enables better addressing of issues concerning the role of the mediator in mediation proceedings.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And how will they be accredited to carry out the mediation?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: These service providers and their personnel will need to be familiar with Ministry's policies and agencies' guidelines in order to provide the best approach and advisories to the parties seeking mediation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: And also, moving along, how about their continuing professional development?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How are they going to be monitored and assessed as well?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: We are talking about commercial cases particularly in this Bill.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For sales disputes, I know that mediators and counsellors have the lemon law as a reference.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: How about for the service industry, which is really quite broad ranging and wide as well?

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: So, mediators covering these cases may need to be informed and empowered in this aspect.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: Also, as we know, in mediation, the choice of mediators plays a critical role.

speaker: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef (Marine Parade)
text: For example, if there is a related case, something pertaining to medical product or service and someone who is conversant and versatile in this area and discipline will be very useful to have as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Murali Pillai sought clarification on whether the Bill is intended to promote mediation as a mainstream form of dispute resolution mechanism as opposed to being an "alternative" dispute resolution option.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If so, he suggested that parties can be encouraged to turn to pre-action mediation to resolve their disputes, before resorting to litigation or arbitration, through: (a) allowing an extension of time limits on a claim where this is being mediated; and (b) extending legal aid to cover mediation, and requiring aided persons to comply with advice by their assigned solicitors to submit their cases for mediation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: First, on the question of what type of dispute resolution, our position has always been to encourage parties to find the most "appropriate" dispute resolution mechanism.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, it is still an "a": it is not "alternative", but "appropriate".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If you think about it, what we have been doing is that we offer different products.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You can have arbitration and litigation, and mediation complements the other two.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, there is a lot of flexibility there, and it is really what suits the parties' needs.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Yet, as the Member has pointed out, it is important to balance a pro-mediation approach against party autonomy to choose for themselves which dispute resolution option best suits their needs, and not to unduly restrict individuals' rights of access to Court, or where they have agreed to other dispute resolution options, such as arbitration.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, in short, we offer an array of options, and parties can pick and choose whatever suits them best.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On the issue of extension of limitation periods, this will require careful study.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In the majority of cases, however, it is unlikely that an ongoing mediation would have any great impact on a limitation period, given that mediation typically is a quick process.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are also existing incentives in the Court process to encourage parties to settle.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Mediation Bill itself will introduce provisions to support an application to stay Court proceedings, on the basis of a mediation agreement, a point noted by many of the Members who spoke.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Court may also take into account parties' attempts to settle for costs of Court proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And parties are also actively encouraged to consider mediation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For cases in the State Courts, disputes may be referred for mediation at the State Courts Centre for Dispute Resolution.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: New changes under the Supreme Court's Practice Directions also encourage lawyers and parties to consider if mediation is appropriate for their case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If we were to extend limitation periods, where mediation takes place, this wider context would have to be considered.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: There are also existing incentives for aided litigants to consider mediation as a viable dispute resolution option.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Legal Aid Bureau encourages all legally aided applicants to settle their disputes amicably.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: That makes sense because it saves time, it saves cost.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Only if mediation is not successful or not possible, for example, because the other party does not wish to mediate or does not turn up, would the applicant be advised to proceed with litigation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And this is particularly so for family-related proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: If an applicant unreasonably refuses to mediate the matter, and the Legal Aid Bureau is of the view that mediation would be a good way to resolve the dispute at hand, a recommendation can be made to the Legal Aid Board on whether to refuse or cancel aid in the matter.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay and Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef both spoke on the importance of setting standards and professionalisation of the mediation industry.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef also asked if we had considered the issue of specialist mediators.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Flexibility is important in ensuring the industry can develop.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: What we have done is to put in place measures to improve training and standards for the mediation industry, in line with our aim to grow Singapore as an international commercial mediation centre.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For mediation training and research, there is also the Singapore International Dispute Resolution Academy (SIDRA).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: SIDRA is the first regional institution dedicated to thought leadership and training and educational excellence in negotiation and dispute resolution.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As for specialist mediators, both SMC and SIMC have specialist lists of mediators available for parties to choose from.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The specialist mediators span a wide range of industries and sectors, such as banking, finance, family, probate and so on.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Patrick Tay suggested putting in place a grievance system to deal with complaints about mediators, while Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan asked if we will, in due course, establish a form of disciplinary tribunal to govern professional ethics rules for mediators.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The mediation industry is a growing one and a heavy-handed approach may not be the best way to go forward at this point in time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: With greater training and accreditation of mediators by the various mediation institutions, we hope that the mediation community will continue to develop its own approach through professional ethics guidance.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But we will continue to monitor this, as the industry continues to professionalise, and we will finetune our framework as we learn from experience.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Thanaletchmi and Assoc Prof Fatimah Lateef both had questions on designated mediation service providers and certified mediators under the Bill and who will be appointed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The reason for having this criterion is to ensure that the settlement agreements are of a quality that can be readily recorded by the Courts.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For now, trusted institutions like SIMC and SMC will be considered for designation as mediation service providers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The mechanism will be reviewed and may be opened up to more institutions when it has been successfully implemented and becomes more established.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Thanaletchimi asked if the Bill applies to tripartite mediations conducted under the Industrial Relations Act, or mediations conducted under other legislative frameworks, for example, the Family Justice Court under the Women's Charter, or mediations conducted by the Small Claims Tribunal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As explained earlier, this is to prevent inconsistency with existing legislative frameworks and rules guiding those mediations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, our approach is really not a one-size-fits-all.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We encourage mediation for all, but within each type of category of claim or type of action, there may be a more specialist approach.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we have got existing frameworks for existing specialist areas, like family law and industrial relations.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Ms Thanaletchimi also sought clarification on whether the Bill requires the presence of lawyers representing the interests of the parties involved in drafting the mediation agreement.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Bill does not require the presence of lawyers.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is up to the parties as to whether they wish to involve their lawyers in the mediation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: On observations made by Mr Louis Ng on the proposal to extend the existing Legal Profession Act exceptions applicable to arbitration to mediation, I would like to clarify that the exceptions are not broad-based, but will only apply in the circumstances set out in the Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng also sought clarification on clause 12(4)(b) of the Bill, which states that the Court may refuse to record a mediated settlement agreement as an order of Court if "the subject matter of the agreement is not capable of settlement".

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Clause 12(4)(b) of the Bill provides that the Court can refuse to record the mediated settlement agreements if the subject matter clearly cannot be resolved through mediation, for example, if the subject matter is illegal.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, if you have a dispute and let us say, for some reason, the two parties agree that the way to resolve that dispute is to go and cheat a third person.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Louis Ng had a question on whether the mediation process will be affected by the proposed changes from the Civil Law (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Third-party funding under the Civil Law (Amendment) Bill will only be extended to mediation proceedings arising out of or in any way connected with international arbitration proceedings, but not to standalone mediation proceedings.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan noted that some aspects of the Bill are a nod to the existing UNCITRAL Model Law on International Commercial Conciliation 2002, the 2002 Model Law, and asked about our position on the ongoing work of the UNCITRAL Working Group II (Dispute Settlement) on the preparation of an instrument on the enforcement of international commercial settlement agreements resulting from conciliation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We have taken the 2002 Model Law into account in crafting the Bill.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As the Member has noted, parts of the Bill take reference from the model provisions contained in the 2002 Model Law, which addresses procedural aspects of a conciliation or mediation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As for the ongoing work of UNCITRAL Working Group II, Singapore has actively participated in those discussions and will continue to do so.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The upcoming 66th Working Group II session will take place in February, where the Working Group will be discussing both the form and substance of the proposed instrument.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: As regard to whether the Bill's restrictions on confidentiality will affect Member of Parliament or agency referrals to community mediation, the Bill will exclude community mediations, that is, those conducted under the Community Mediation Centre (CMC) or the Community Dispute Resolution Tribunal (CDRT).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: These will continue to be regulated by the legislation and rules that apply to those mediations today.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For referrals to the CMC, Members of Parliament and agencies will be updated on the outcome of such referrals.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The terms of the agreement, however, remain confidential.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I would like, once again, to thank them for their strong support for this Bill, which is yet another step forward in helping Singapore grow as a dispute resolution centre.
